column1: ubiquitous|/juːˈbɪkwɪtəs/|FORMAL|C2|Present, appearing, or found everywhere at once.|High-frequency GRE adjective for pervasive trends, tools, or phenomena.|Smartphone cameras have become so ubiquitous that almost every public event is documented instantly.|omnipresent,pervasive,universal~rare,scarce

ephemeral|/ɪˈfɛmərəl/|FORMAL|C2|Lasting for only a very brief period of time.|Evokes fleeting beauty or short-lived viral hype in formal writing.|Viral internet fame is notoriously ephemeral unless creators build lasting trust.|fleeting,transient,short-lived~enduring,perpetual

laconic|/ləˈkɑːnɪk/|FORMAL|C2|Using very few words; concisely and sometimes bluntly brief.|Named after Laconia (Sparta), famous for terse, no-nonsense replies.|Her laconic email—just "Approved, ship it"—told us everything we needed to know.|terse,succinct,concise~verbose,garrulous

pragmatic|/præɡˈmætɪk/|PROFESSIONAL|C1|Dealing with problems sensibly and realistically rather than theoretically.|Essential in both GRE passages and American executive discussions.|We took a pragmatic approach and shipped the core workflow before polishing edge cases.|practical,realistic,sensible~idealistic,impractical

equivocal|/ɪˈkwɪvəkəl/|FORMAL|C2|Open to more than one interpretation; deliberately ambiguous or uncertain.|Often critiques hedged answers, mixed study results, or cautious politicians.|The clinical trial yielded equivocal findings, prompting researchers to expand the sample.|ambiguous,unclear,evasive~unequivocal,decisive

magnanimous|/mæɡˈnænɪməs/|FORMAL|C2|Generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful.|Literally "great-souled" from Latin; signals gracious victory or leadership.|In a magnanimous gesture after the debate, she praised her opponent's community work.|generous,gracious,chivalrous~petty,vindictive

obsequious|/əbˈsiːkwiəs/|FORMAL|C2|Obedient or attentive to an excessive, self-serving degree.|Strongly critical GRE term for flattery aimed at winning favor.|The junior aide's obsequious praise made the director visibly uncomfortable.|sycophantic,fawning,servile~assertive,independent

perfunctory|/pərˈfʌŋktəri/|FORMAL|C2|Carried out with minimal effort, care, or genuine reflection.|Ideal for describing box-checking reviews or half-hearted apologies.|He gave the proposal only a perfunctory glance before asking the team to rewrite it.|cursory,superficial,mechanical~thorough,meticulous

recalcitrant|/rɪˈkælsɪtrənt/|FORMAL|C2|Stubbornly uncooperative or resistant to authority and change.|From Latin meaning "kicking back with the heels"; formal and pointed.|Several recalcitrant committee members delayed the safety policy for months.|defiant,unruly,obstinate~compliant,amenable

sycophant|/ˈsɪkəfænt/|FORMAL|C2|A person who flatters powerful people solely to gain personal advantage.|Classic GRE noun describing yes-men in politics or corporate life.|Strong leaders surround themselves with candid critics rather than sycophants.|flatterer,toady,yes-man~critic,detractor

taciturn|/ˈtæsɪtɜːrn/|FORMAL|C2|Reserved or uncommunicative in speech; saying little by temperament.|Neutral-to-observational term for quiet people, softer than unfriendly.|Though taciturn in large meetings, he shares remarkably sharp insights one-on-one.|reticent,reserved,uncommunicative~loquacious,talkative

veracity|/vəˈræsəti/|FORMAL|C2|Conformity to facts; habitual truthfulness and accuracy.|Frequently tested in GRE reading comprehension about sources and evidence.|Editors spent three days verifying the veracity of the whistleblower's documents.|truthfulness,accuracy,credibility~falsehood,mendacity

alacrity|/əˈlækrəti/|FORMAL|C2|Brisk, cheerful readiness and eager willingness to act.|Always carries a positive, energetic tone when paired with "with alacrity."|She accepted the fellowship offer with alacrity and began relocating that week.|eagerness,promptness,enthusiasm~reluctance,apathy

ameliorate|/əˈmiːliəreɪt/|FORMAL|C2|To make a bad, painful, or unsatisfactory situation better.|Formal academic verb exclusively used for improving negative conditions.|Expanded transit subsidies helped ameliorate commuting costs for hourly workers.|improve,alleviate,mitigate~worsen,aggravate

anachronism|/əˈnækrənɪzəm/|FORMAL|C2|Something belonging to a different historical period than the one in which it appears.|Used both for historical film errors and outdated traditions.|Typing memos on carbon paper feels like a charming anachronism in a cloud-first office.|throwback,relic,misplacement~innovation,modernity

apathy|/ˈæpəθi/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Lack of interest, enthusiasm, or emotional concern.|Core GRE word in civic, sociological, and workplace commentary.|Low voter turnout reflected growing apathy toward repetitive campaign promises.|indifference,detachment,unconcern~passion,engagement

austere|/ɔːˈstɪr/|FORMAL|C2|Severe, strict in manner, or starkly plain without decoration or luxury.|Applies equally to minimalist architecture, tight budgets, or stern personalities.|The monastery's austere dining hall contained nothing but oak benches and white walls.|stark,spartan,severe~ornate,lavish

banal|/bəˈnæl/|FORMAL|C2|So lacking in originality as to be obvious, predictable, and boring.|Sharp literary critique of cliched speeches, plots, or advice.|The keynote promised bold disruption but delivered mostly banal productivity slogans.|trite,hackneyed,cliched~original,inventive

capricious|/kəˈprɪʃəs/|FORMAL|C2|Given to sudden, unaccountable changes of mood, policy, or behavior.|Useful for unpredictable weather, markets, or erratic decision-makers.|Investors grew wary of the regulator's capricious shifts in licensing rules.|whimsical,erratic,fickle~consistent,steadfast

caustic|/ˈkɔːstɪk/|FORMAL|C2|Sarcastic in a scathing, biting, or bitterly critical way.|Originally referred to chemically burning substances; metaphorical for sharp wit.|The theater critic's caustic review spared neither the script nor the lighting design.|acerbic,biting,mordant~gentle,complimentary

cogent|/ˈkoʊdʒənt/|FORMAL|C2|Clear, logical, and genuinely convincing.|One of the highest compliments for an essay, legal brief, or argument.|She laid out a cogent case for phasing out legacy servers before peak season.|compelling,persuasive,lucid~unconvincing,muddled

corroborate|/kəˈrɑːbəreɪt/|FORMAL|C1|To confirm or give independent support to a statement, theory, or finding.|Standard in journalism, science, law, and GRE analytical passages.|Satellite imagery corroborated the field team's report of rapid glacier melt.|confirm,substantiate,verify~contradict,refute

dearth|/dɜːrθ/|FORMAL|C2|A scarcity or noticeable lack of something needed.|Concise formal substitute for "severe shortage" in academic prose.|There is no dearth of opinions online, yet reliable primary data remains scarce.|scarcity,shortage,paucity~abundance,surplus

deference|/ˈdɛfərəns/|FORMAL|C2|Humble submission and polite respect shown to someone's judgment or status.|Often appears in the phrase "in deference to" in formal English.|Out of deference to the departing founder, the board delayed announcing the rebrand.|respect,regard,reverence~disrespect,defiance

derivative|/dɪˈrɪvətɪv/|FORMAL|C1|Imitative of another work and lacking genuine originality.|Critical tone in art, cinema, and tech reviews.|Critics dismissed the sequel as a derivative rehash of the original film's plot.|unoriginal,imitative,secondhand~original,groundbreaking

desiccate|/ˈdɛsɪkeɪt/|FORMAL|C2|To remove moisture thoroughly; metaphorically, to drain of vitality.|Appears in both ecology passages and literary descriptions of dry prose.|Months of drought desiccated the valley soil and withered the orchards.|dehydrate,parch,dry out~hydrate,moisten

diatribe|/ˈdaɪətraɪb/|FORMAL|C2|A forceful, bitter verbal or written attack against someone or something.|Stronger and longer than a complaint; implies a heated tirade.|What began as a budget question spiraled into a ten-minute diatribe against management.|tirade,harangue,screed~praise,encomium

diffident|/ˈdɪfɪdənt/|FORMAL|C2|Modest or shy because of a lack of self-confidence.|Commonly misread as "indifferent"—actually means hesitant and self-doubting.|Once diffident about public speaking, he now leads quarterly town halls effortlessly.|timid,hesitant,self-effacing~confident,assertive

dilatory|/ˈdɪlətɔːri/|FORMAL|C2|Slow to act; intended to cause delay or stall a process.|Formal legal and administrative term for foot-dragging.|The defense employed dilatory motions to push the hearing past the election.|stalling,sluggish,procrastinating~prompt,expeditious

disparage|/dɪˈspærɪdʒ/|FORMAL|C1|To regard or represent someone or something as being of little worth.|Polished alternative to "put down" or "belittle" in formal discourse.|Healthy competition pushes teams forward without needing to disparage rivals.|belittle,denigrate,deprecate~praise,extol

dogmatic|/dɔːɡˈmætɪk/|FORMAL|C1|Inclined to lay down principles as undeniably true without considering evidence.|Frequent GRE critique of rigid thinkers in science and politics.|Good researchers remain skeptical rather than dogmatic when new data challenges theory.|rigid,doctrinaire,inflexible~open-minded,pragmatic

ebullient|/ɪˈbʊljənt/|FORMAL|C2|Cheerful, buoyant, and overflowing with lively energy.|Literally "boiling over" from Latin; vivid descriptor for celebratory moods.|The lab team was ebullient after their prototype passed every endurance test.|exuberant,buoyant,vivacious~gloomy,subdued

eclectic|/ɪˈklɛktɪk/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Deriving ideas, style, or taste from a broad and diverse range of sources.|Positive, cultured adjective for playlists, architecture, or reading habits.|The bookstore curates an eclectic mix of graphic novels, history, and indie zines.|diverse,varied,wide-ranging~uniform,narrow

efficacious|/ˌɛfɪˈkeɪʃəs/|FORMAL|C2|Successful in producing a desired or intended result.|Preferred in medical, policy, and academic contexts over plain "effective."|Early literacy coaching proved remarkably efficacious in narrowing reading gaps.|effective,potent,productive~ineffective,futile

elegy|/ˈɛlədʒi/|FORMAL|C2|A poem or reflective piece of serious mourning, especially for someone deceased.|Common GRE literary term; also used figuratively for vanished eras.|Her memoir reads like an elegy for the small industrial towns of the Midwest.|lament,requiem,dirge~celebration,paean

elicit|/ɪˈlɪsɪt/|PROFESSIONAL|C1|To draw out or evoke a response, answer, or reaction from someone.|Careful not to confuse with "illicit" (illegal); very common in research and interviews.|Open-ended questions elicit far richer customer feedback than yes-or-no surveys.|evoke,draw out,prompt~suppress,stifle

embellish|/ɪmˈbɛlɪʃ/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|To decorate or enhance, often by adding exaggerated details to a story.|Can be neutral (design) or mildly critical (stretching the truth).|He tends to embellish his fishing stories until a trout sounds like a marlin.|adorn,ornament,exaggerate~simplify,understate

empirical|/ɪmˈpɪrɪkəl/|FORMAL|C1|Based on observation, measurement, or experiment rather than pure theory.|Cornerstone GRE vocabulary for scientific and economic reasoning.|The policy debate shifted once empirical evidence from three cities arrived.|observational,experimental,data-driven~theoretical,speculative

emulate|/ˈɛmjuleɪt/|PROFESSIONAL|C1|To match or surpass a person or achievement, typically through admiration and imitation.|Elevated cousin of "imitate" with an aspirational, respectful tone.|Startups across the region tried to emulate the studio's transparent hiring process.|imitate,mirror,model after~reject,shun

enervate|/ˈɛnərveɪt/|FORMAL|C2|To cause someone to feel drained of energy or vitality.|Tricky GRE trap word—looks like "energize" but means the exact opposite!|Three hours of humid midday heat enervated even the most seasoned marathoners.|exhaust,sap,weaken~invigorate,energize

engender|/ɪnˈdʒɛndər/|FORMAL|C2|To cause or give rise to a feeling, situation, or condition.|Crisp academic verb for linking causes to social or emotional outcomes.|Consistent transparency engenders lasting trust during organizational transitions.|generate,spark,foster~quell,prevent

enigmatic|/ˌɛnɪɡˈmætɪk/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Difficult to interpret or understand; mysteriously intriguing.|From "enigma" (riddle); common in arts criticism and character profiles.|She left an enigmatic note on the whiteboard and vanished before lunch.|mysterious,cryptic,inscrutable~transparent,obvious

ennui|/ɑːnˈwiː/|FORMAL|C2|A feeling of listlessness and dissatisfaction arising from boredom or lack of purpose.|French loanword used in literary criticism and cultural essays.|After months of repetitive data entry, a heavy sense of ennui set in.|weariness,boredom,tedium~excitement,vitality

erudite|/ˈɛrjudaɪt/|FORMAL|C2|Having or showing great scholarly knowledge and deep learning.|High-register compliment for professors, historians, and well-researched books.|Her erudite commentary connected nineteenth-century tariffs to modern supply chains.|scholarly,learned,well-read~uninformed,ignorant

esoteric|/ˌɛsəˈtɛrɪk/|FORMAL|C2|Intended for or likely to be understood by only a small group with specialized knowledge.|Frequently used to describe niche jargon, theory, or cult hobbies.|The seminar drifted into esoteric tax clauses that lost half the audience.|arcane,obscure,niche~mainstream,accessible

eulogy|/ˈjuːlədʒi/|FORMAL|C1|A speech or piece of writing that praises someone highly, especially after their death.|From Greek roots meaning "good speech"; also used metaphorically for tributes.|His heartfelt eulogy celebrated his grandmother's humor and fierce generosity.|tribute,panegyric,encomium~criticism,denunciation

exacerbate|/ɪɡˈzæsərbeɪt/|PROFESSIONAL|C1|To make an existing problem, bad situation, or negative feeling worse.|Widely used in journalism, medicine, and policy discussions.|Unplanned scope changes only exacerbated the engineering team's burnout.|worsen,aggravate,intensify~alleviate,ameliorate

exculpate|/ˈɛkskʌlpeɪt/|FORMAL|C2|To show or declare that someone is not guilty of wrongdoing.|Legal and analytical GRE favorite derived from Latin "culpa" (blame).|Timestamped server logs completely exculpated the contractor from the outage.|absolve,clear,vindicate~incriminate,blame

exigency|/ˈɛksɪdʒənsi/|FORMAL|C2|An urgent need, demand, or pressing situation requiring immediate action.|Formal noun often seen in plural ("the exigencies of wartime logistics").|Budget exigencies forced the museum to postpone its east-wing renovation.|urgency,necessity,crisis~luxury,leisure

exonerate|/ɪɡˈzɑːnəreɪt/|FORMAL|C1|To absolve someone officially from blame, fault, or criminal accusation.|Closely related to exculpate, especially for formal legal or institutional clearance.|DNA testing ultimately exonerated the defendant after twelve years of appeals.|acquit,vindicate,clear~convict,condemn

expeditious|/ˌɛkspəˈdɪʃəs/|FORMAL|C2|Done with speed, efficiency, and minimal bureaucratic friction.|Formal upgrade for "fast and smooth" in legal or operational writing.|We appreciate the customs office's expeditious clearance of the medical shipment.|prompt,swift,efficient~dilatory,sluggish

extemporaneous|/ɪkˌstɛmpəˈreɪniəs/|FORMAL|C2|Spoken or done without prior scripting or formal preparation.|Classic GRE word for off-the-cuff speeches and improvised remarks.|Despite losing his slides, he delivered a poised extemporaneous keynote.|impromptu,improvised,unscripted~rehearsed,scripted

facetious|/fəˈsiːʃəs/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Treating serious issues with deliberately inappropriate or playful humor.|Handy when clarifying that a sarcastic remark wasn't meant literally.|I was only being facetious when I suggested solving traffic with zip lines.|flippant,tongue-in-cheek,glib~earnest,sincere

fallacious|/fəˈleɪʃəs/|FORMAL|C2|Based on a mistaken belief or flawed logical reasoning.|Directly tied to "fallacy"; core word for GRE analytical writing.|Relying on two cherry-picked anecdotes leads to a fallacious conclusion.|flawed,erroneous,unsound~valid,sound

fastidious|/fæˈstɪdiəs/|FORMAL|C2|Very attentive to and concerned about accuracy, cleanliness, and tiny details.|Can be admiring (craftsmanship) or mildly amused (picky habits).|The watchmaker was fastidious about keeping even microscopic dust off the gears.|meticulous,scrupulous,fussy~careless,sloppy

fawn|/fɔːn/|FORMAL|C2|To give an exaggerated display of affection or flattery to win favor.|Almost always paired with "over" ("fawn over celebrities").|Reporters refused to fawn over the tech founder and pressed him on privacy.|flatter,grovel,kowtow~snub,criticize

felicitous|/fəˈlɪsɪtəs/|FORMAL|C2|Well-chosen, apt, and pleasingly suited to the occasion.|Frequent GRE word for graceful phrasing or fortunate timing.|Her felicitous phrasing turned a tense apology into a unifying moment.|apt,fitting,well-chosen~awkward,inapt

fervor|/ˈfɜːrvər/|FORMAL|C1|Intense, passionate feeling or ardent enthusiasm.|Elevated literary noun for conviction, activism, or artistic devotion.|Volunteers canvassed the neighborhood with remarkable fervor despite the rain.|passion,ardor,zeal~apathy,indifference

flagrant|/ˈfleɪɡrənt/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Conspicuously, shockingly, or unmistakably offensive and blatant.|Common in sports ("flagrant foul"), law, and ethics reporting.|Ignoring three safety inspections was a flagrant violation of building codes.|blatant,glaring,egregious~subtle,minor

foment|/foʊˈmɛnt/|FORMAL|C2|To instigate or stir up undesirable sentiment, unrest, or conflict.|Almost exclusively carries a negative, provocative connotation.|Anonymous accounts attempted to foment distrust ahead of the union vote.|incite,provoke,instigate~quell,pacify

forestall|/fɔːrˈstɔːl/|FORMAL|C2|To prevent or obstruct something by taking proactive action ahead of time.|Crisp verb for heading off crises before they materialize.|Transparent Q&A memos helped forestall rumors about the merger.|preempt,avert,prevent~provoke,invite

frugality|/fruːˈɡæləti/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|The quality of being economical and careful with money or resources.|Positive or neutral; contrasts with stinginess by emphasizing smart stewardship.|Years of disciplined frugality allowed the founders to bootstrap without debt.|thrift,economy,prudence~extravagance,waste

garrulous|/ˈɡærələs/|FORMAL|C2|Excessively talkative, especially about trivial or meandering matters.|Classic antonym of "laconic" and "taciturn" on GRE verbal exams.|Our garrulous cab driver recounted forty years of neighborhood history before we arrived.|loquacious,chatty,verbose~taciturn,laconic

gregarious|/ɡrɪˈɡɛriəs/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Fond of company; naturally sociable and energized by groups.|Applies to both outgoing people and social animal species.|Being naturally gregarious, she turned every conference coffee line into a reunion.|sociable,outgoing,convivial~reclusive,introverted

guile|/ɡaɪl/|FORMAL|C2|Sly, cunning intelligence used to deceive or manipulate others.|Often appears in its negative form "guileless" (innocent and transparent).|He won the negotiation through transparent math rather than courtroom guile.|cunning,artifice,duplicity~candor,honesty

hackneyed|/ˈhækniːd/|FORMAL|C2|Overused to the point of losing freshness, impact, or originality.|Editor's favorite critique of tired metaphors and corporate buzzwords.|Skip the hackneyed "think outside the box" line and show concrete examples.|cliched,trite,stale~fresh,original

harangue|/həˈræŋ/|FORMAL|C2|A lengthy, aggressive, or lecturing speech aimed at scolding an audience.|Works as both noun and verb; stronger and louder than a simple critique.|The coach's halftime harangue echoed all the way down the stadium tunnel.|tirade,diatribe,lecture~praise,compliment

hedonist|/ˈhiːdənɪst/|FORMAL|C1|A person who believes that the pursuit of pleasure is the highest goal in life.|Philosophical and cultural term ranging from lighthearted foodie to indulgent.|He joked that he became a weekend hedonist the moment he discovered pastries in Lyon.|pleasure-seeker,epicure,sybarite~ascetic,puritan

iconoclast|/aɪˈkɑːnəklæst/|FORMAL|C2|A person who challenges or attacks cherished beliefs, traditions, or institutions.|Originally meant breaker of religious icons; now used for bold innovators.|As an architectural iconoclast, she rejected glass towers in favor of timber domes.|rebel,maverick,nonconformist~conformist,traditionalist

idiosyncratic|/ˌɪdiəsɪŋˈkrætɪk/|FORMAL|C2|Peculiar or distinctive to a specific individual; delightfully or oddly unique.|Neutral-to-affectionate word for personal quirks and unmistakable styles.|The director's idiosyncratic pacing makes every film immediately recognizable.|quirky,distinctive,unconventional~conventional,typical

immutable|/ɪˈmjuːtəbl/|FORMAL|C2|Unchanging over time or unable to be altered.|Used in philosophy, law, and software engineering ("immutable ledger").|Cultural norms shift every decade; very few workplace rules are truly immutable.|unchangeable,fixed,permanent~mutable,variable

impair|/ɪmˈpɛr/|PROFESSIONAL|C1|To weaken, diminish, or damage the functioning of something.|Standard in health, finance, and technical risk assessments.|Chronic sleep deprivation can severely impair judgment and reaction times.|weaken,diminish,undermine~enhance,strengthen

impassive|/ɪmˈpæsɪv/|FORMAL|C2|Not showing or feeling outward emotion; calm and expressionless.|Often describes poker players, judges, or composed negotiators.|She remained completely impassive while listening to the rival bid.|stoic,unemotional,deadpan~expressive,emotional

impecunious|/ˌɪmpɪˈkjuːniəs/|FORMAL|C2|Having little or no money; chronically short of funds.|Literary, slightly wry GRE word rooted in Latin "pecunia" (money).|Even as an impecunious graduate student, he never missed a library book sale.|penniless,destitute,strapped~affluent,wealthy

impede|/ɪmˈpiːd/|PROFESSIONAL|C1|To delay, obstruct, or slow down progress or movement.|Crisp formal alternative to "hold back" or "get in the way of."|Overly complex approval chains impede fast collaboration across time zones.|hinder,obstruct,hamper~facilitate,expedite

impermeable|/ɪmˈpɜːrmiəbl/|FORMAL|C1|Not allowing fluid, ideas, or influence to pass through.|Works both physically (raincoats, clay) and figuratively (closed cliques).|The jacket's impermeable shell kept us dry through an hour-long downpour.|waterproof,impenetrable,sealed~porous,permeable

imperturbable|/ˌɪmpərˈtɜːrbəbl/|FORMAL|C2|Unable to be upset, rattled, or excited; remarkably calm under pressure.|High praise for crisis managers, pilots, and composed leaders.|Even when the livestream crashed mid-launch, the producer stayed imperturbable.|unflappable,serene,composed~excitable,anxious

impervious|/ɪmˈpɜːrviəs/|FORMAL|C2|Unable to be affected, penetrated, or influenced by something.|Frequently paired with "to" ("impervious to criticism" or "impervious to rain").|He seemed completely impervious to online heckling and kept shipping new work.|immune,unaffected,resistant~susceptible,vulnerable

implacable|/ɪmˈplækəbl/|FORMAL|C2|Unable to be appeased, calmed, or persuaded to soften opposition.|Intense GRE word for relentless foes, critics, or forces of nature.|The senator remained an implacable opponent of privatizing public parks.|relentless,unyielding,unforgiving~forgiving,placable

implicit|/ɪmˈplɪsɪt/|PROFESSIONAL|C1|Suggested or understood though not directly stated in words.|Essential pair with "explicit" in contracts, culture, and research.|There was an implicit understanding that nobody scheduled calls on Friday afternoons.|implied,unspoken,tacit~explicit,stated

implode|/ɪmˈploʊd/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|To collapse violently inward; figuratively, to fail catastrophically from within.|Vivid journalism verb for failing startups, alliances, or shaky plans.|Without basic accounting controls, the fast-growing venture imploded within a year.|collapse,crumble,cave in~expand,thrive

inadvertently|/ˌɪnədˈvɜːrtəntli/|PROFESSIONAL|C1|Without intention; accidentally or through oversight.|Polite, precise word for owning mistakes in professional emails.|We inadvertently omitted the appendix from the draft and have attached it now.|accidentally,unintentionally,unwittingly~deliberately,intentionally

inchoate|/ɪnˈkoʊət/|FORMAL|C2|Just begun and not yet fully formed, organized, or developed.|Classic GRE adjective for early-stage ideas, movements, or drafts.|Her notebook was filled with inchoate sketches that eventually became an acclaimed novel.|nascent,rudimentary,unformed~mature,developed

incongruous|/ɪnˈkɑːŋɡruəs/|FORMAL|C2|Out of place or not in harmony with the surroundings or context.|Great descriptive word for humorous or jarring visual/tonal contrasts.|A neon arcade machine looked wonderfully incongruous inside the historic Victorian library.|out of place,mismatched,jarring~harmonious,fitting

inconsequential|/ɪnˌkɑːnsɪˈkwɛnʃəl/|PROFESSIONAL|C1|Not important or significant enough to affect the outcome.|Useful for separating noise from real priorities in analysis.|Minor formatting tweaks are inconsequential compared with fixing the checkout latency.|trivial,negligible,minor~significant,momentous

indeterminate|/ˌɪndɪˈtɜːrmɪnət/|FORMAL|C2|Not exactly known, established, or defined.|Formal academic adjective for open-ended timelines or inconclusive measurements.|The excavation was paused for an indeterminate period due to seasonal flooding.|uncertain,unspecified,indefinite~definite,fixed

indigence|/ˈɪndɪdʒəns/|FORMAL|C2|A state of extreme poverty and severe financial need.|Classic GRE noun frequently contrasted with affluence or opulence.|Municipal food banks expanded rapidly to relieve winter indigence.|poverty,destitution,penury~affluence,wealth

indolent|/ˈɪndələnt/|FORMAL|C2|Wanting to avoid activity or exertion; habitually lazy.|More literary and polished than plain "lazy"; often used for warm afternoons too.|An indolent Sunday afternoon in a hammock was exactly what she needed.|slothful,idle,lethargic~industrious,diligent

inert|/ɪˈnɜːrt/|FORMAL|C1|Lacking the ability or strength to move; chemically or socially inactive.|Used in chemistry ("inert gas") and metaphorically for sluggish committees.|Without a clear owner, the initiative sat completely inert for two quarters.|motionless,inactive,dormant~active,dynamic

ingenuous|/ɪnˈdʒɛnjuəs/|FORMAL|C2|Innocent, candid, and unsuspecting—not to be confused with "ingenious."|Famous GRE confusable pair: ingenuous = candid/naive; ingenious = clever!|Her ingenuous curiosity disarmed even the most guarded interviewees.|candid,artless,naive~disingenuous,calculating

inherent|/ɪnˈhɪrənt/|PROFESSIONAL|C1|Existing in something as a permanent, essential, or built-in attribute.|Cornerstone analytical adjective in law, policy, and engineering.|Every ambitious product migration carries some inherent operational risk.|intrinsic,innate,built-in~extrinsic,incidental

innocuous|/ɪˈnɑːkjuəs/|FORMAL|C2|Not harmful, offensive, or likely to provoke trouble.|Great for distinguishing harmless remarks from loaded critiques.|What looked like an innocuous config tweak accidentally broke mobile logins.|harmless,benign,inoffensive~harmful,pernicious

insensible|/ɪnˈsɛnsəbl/|FORMAL|C2|Unaware of, indifferent to, or numbed against physical or emotional sensation.|Formal nuance: often means "oblivious to" rather than literally unconscious.|He seemed insensible to the tension building across the conference table.|oblivious,unaware,numb~sensitive,attuned

insinuate|/ɪnˈsɪnjueɪt/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|To suggest or hint at something unpleasant in an indirect, sly way.|Almost always carries a negative or suspicious connotation.|Are you trying to insinuate that the audit figures were deliberately rounded?|imply,hint,intimate~state directly,declare
